content: There are two primary types of diabetes. Type 1 diabetes typically affects younger individuals and requires treatment with insulin injections. In contrast, Type 2 diabetes generally affects older individuals and can often be managed with dietary modifications and oral medications. Diabetic neuropathy, a common complication of diabetes, is present in approximately 10% of patients at the time of diagnosis and increases to 40-50% after 10 years of living with the disease. Enhanced glucose control has been extensively studied as a potential intervention to prevent this debilitating condition, but no systematic reviews of the evidence had been conducted prior to this analysis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the evidence supporting the use of enhanced glucose control to prevent distal symmetric polyneuropathy in individuals with Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating enhanced glycemic control in diabetes mellitus. The search included studies published up to January 2012. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomized, controlled studies that assessed enhanced glycemic control and reported neuropathy outcomes after at least one year of intervention. The primary outcome of interest was the annual incidence of clinical neuropathy, as defined by a clinical scale. Secondary outcomes included motor nerve conduction velocity and quantitative vibration testing. Two independent reviewers screened the studies for inclusion, extracted data using a standardized form, and resolved any disagreements with the help of a third reviewer. The data were analyzed using annualized risk differences (RDs) for clinical neuropathy and mean differences per year for conduction velocity and vibration threshold measurements. Seventeen randomized studies were included in the review. Of these, seven studies focused on individuals with Type 1 diabetes, eight on those with Type 2 diabetes, and two included participants with both types. A meta-analysis of two studies involving 1,228 participants with Type 1 diabetes demonstrated that enhanced glucose control significantly reduced the risk of developing clinical neuropathy. The annualized risk difference was -1.84% (95% confidence interval [CI]: -1.11% to -2.56%). Similarly, a meta-analysis of four studies involving 6,669 participants with Type 2 diabetes showed a reduction in the annualized risk of developing clinical neuropathy, with an RD of -0.58% (95% CI: -0.01% to -1.17%). However, this result was not formally statistically significant (P = 0.06). Secondary outcomes, including motor nerve conduction velocity and vibration threshold testing, showed significant improvements in favor of intensive glucose control in both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes populations. However, the review also found that enhanced glucose control was associated with a significant increase in severe adverse events, particularly hypoglycemic episodes, in both groups. In conclusion, high-quality evidence indicates that enhanced glucose control significantly reduces the risk of developing clinical neuropathy and improves nerve conduction and vibration threshold abnormalities in individuals with Type 1 diabetes. For individuals with Type 2 diabetes, enhanced glucose control also reduces the incidence of clinical neuropathy, although this reduction did not reach formal statistical significance. Nevertheless, enhanced glucose control significantly improves nerve conduction and vibration threshold abnormalities in this population. Importantly, the increased risk of severe hypoglycemic events associated with intensive glucose control must be carefully considered when weighing the risks and benefits of this intervention.
